newsitem.title: USA: NASA works on plans to repair tattered telescope.
newsitem.headline: NASA works on plans to repair tattered telescope.

text.p: NASA worked on plans to patch up the Hubble Space Telescope's torn and tattered exterior on Sunday as shuttle Discovery's astronauts completed another day's work on the orbiting observatory.

Rips and tears in the silvery foil covering much of the telescope's exterior were serious enough for officials to consider delaying the fourth and final spacewalk of the mission or adding a fifth to make repairs.
Scientists were concerned the damaged material could peel off and contaminate the telescope's delicate optics.
"They do have some fairly significant concerns with these areas and therefore I'm seriously considering trying do some repair," flight director Jeff Bantle told the crew.
Engineers and astronauts on the ground devised a plan to tie patches over four areas of the telescope's exterior, including one long rip in the foil close to the top of the telescope.
Jerry Ross, a veteran of four spacewalks, was to try out the procedure on a mock-up of the telescope in a water tank close to the Johnson Space Centre.

Bantle favoured delaying Sunday's planned spacewalk by one day so astronauts could fashion blankets from strips of insulation, but Shuttle commander Ken Bowersox urged him to consider adding a fifth spacewalk to make the repairs.
"I think it would be better to keep pressing along nominally and use that contingency day that's in the plan" for a fifth spacewalk, Bowersox said.
Mission managers were to meet later on Sunday morning to decide a course of action.
Earlier, Mark Lee and Steve Smith, making the third spacewalk of the mission, took a close-up look at some of the damage.

"Basically this thing is just falling apart, cracking all over the place," Lee told mission control, as he inspected a foil-covered door on the telescope. The tattered material did not appear to be brittle, he added.
Lee tried taping up a crack, but as NASA engineers had suspected, the adhesive failed to work.
"It barely sticks," he said. "It doesn't do anything."
Lee and Smith collected pieces of spare foil, tape and cords for the possible repair.

Engineers suspected that variations in temperature and ultraviolet rays from the sun had caused the silvery foil to crack and tear. The damage, which appeared extensive, was not seen when astronauts last visited the telescope in 1993.

Lee and Smith upgraded three more components of the telescope during their seven-hour spacewalk. They completed what was considered the most challenging task of the effort, the replacement of a faulty electronics box.

The replacement of the data interface unit, which relays computer commands to various telescope components, was difficult because the device was not designed to be handled by astronauts wearing bulky space suit gloves.
Working in a jumble of wires, Lee had to make 18 cable connections to complete the installation.
"Great hands, Mark," mission control's Jeff Hoffman radioed once the work was done.
The two men then went on to exchange an ageing reel-to-reel tape recorder for a new digital model and replace a broken flywheel, used to manoeuvre the telescope.
"You guys are batting 100 percent," mission control's Marc Garneau radioed as the two men completed their work.
Between tasks, the astronauts marvelled at the spectacular view as the shuttle soared more than 370 miles (595 km) above the Pacific, off the west coast of Australia.
"Holy cow!" Lee exclaimed. "I've got the Hubble Space Telescope, Shark's Bay, and the planet Earth and the moon in my view. What a great place to be."
"Just an average day for a couple of spacewalkers," Joe Tanner remarked from inside the shuttle's cabin.

As the astronauts ended their spacewalk, shuttle commander Ken Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz fired the shuttle's smallest manoeuvring jets for 20 minutes to nudge the Hubble into a higher orbit.
NASA hopes to boost the telescope's altitude by a total of five miles (8 km) to prolong its lifetime.
